newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Fear of violence hurts Bethlehem tourist trade.
newsitem.headline: Fear of violence hurts Bethlehem tourist trade.

text.p: Joseph Canavati anticipated a joyous Christmas when he opened his hotel for business after returning to his native Bethlehem from the United States in September.
But Israeli-Palestinian gun battles at the doorstep of the West Bank town where Jesus was born have nearly ruined his newborn business and sapped the holiday spirit.
"I returned home for peace. But things are going from bad to worse," said the 39-year-old Canavati, who left Philadelphia after 18 years to set up a business in Bethlehem.
"Bethlehem is the best place in the world. But unfortunately, tourists look at it as a war zone," he said.

More than three years after Israel and the PLO signed a landmark peace accord, Bethlehem's 40,000 Palestinians have yet to see the dividends of peace. Israel pulled out of Bethlehem just four days before last Christmas. It was the first Christmas there under Palestinian self-rule.

Although they sit on a treasure trove of historic sites that millions of Christians around the world dream of visiting, many businessmen in Bethlehem complain of unfulfilled dreams of prosperity after peace.
Palestinians said only a fraction of the tourists who visit Bethlehem every year stay in the city to shop, dine or even spend a night.

"Tourists come and visit our historic sites but they return and sleep in Israel. We want tourists to stay with us, to shop and dine in our facilities," said George Sammour, director of Tourism Industries and Licensing at the Palestinian Tourism Ministry.
Sammour said about 960,000 tourists have visited Bethlehem this year, down 12 percent from last year.

"Tourism is very much linked to politics. Israel froze the peace process and is driving Palestinians and the whole region to desperation," he said in a reference to the election six months ago of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose commitment to peace has been questioned by Palestinians.

"The political situation and the news that reaches the world on the situation here are damaging tourism not only for us but also to Israel itself," said Bethlehem Mayor Elias Freij, who is also minister of tourism in the Palestinian Authority.

Palestinians' greatest tourist resource remained undeveloped during nearly three decades of Israeli occupation, where military authorities maintained tough restrictions on licensing hotels and restaurants.
Shedding Israeli regulations, the Palestinian Tourism Ministry has encouraged local and expatriate businessmen like Canavati to build hotels and restaurants in town.

In less than two years since Israel handed over responsibility for tourism to the Palestinian Authority, the number of hotels in Bethlehem and surrounding towns has doubled from four to eight. Hotel rooms have grown from around 280 before the 1993 Israeli-PLO self-rule deal to more than 900.
More than 200 rooms are under construction and officials envisage having as many as 3,000 in three years when the town celebrates the 2,000th year since Christ's birth.

Canavati's 36-room Alexander Hotel was the latest addition to the expanding tourist facilities in Bethlehem. A few months before he opened his hotel, the Arja brothers opened the 160-room Bethlehem Hotel next door.
Across the street, only one group of tourists dined at the newly opened Sababa restaurant, one of about 50 in town.
Khader Shoukeh, who owns a restaurant a few hundred metres (yards) from Manger Square, has put his restaurant up for sale.
An unfinished peace accord, political instability and violence continue to stifle tourism for both Israelis and Palestinians.

A wave of Islamic suicide bombings that killed 59 people in Israel in February and March scared many tourists away. An Israeli closure imposed on the West Bank and Gaza because of the attacks aggravated the problem.
Israel's opening of a tourist tunnel near Islamic holy sites in Jerusalem in September ignited renewed violence in which 60 Palestinians and 15 Israelis were killed.
For nearly two weeks, the few tourists who ventured to visit Bethlehem had to walk across the Israeli military checkpoint between the West Bank city and Jerusalem.

"Tourists like to stay in Bethlehem. But they feel annoyed to have to go through security checks or if they have to walk over an army checkpoint," said Doris Awad, front desk and reservations manager at the Bethlehem Hotel.
